extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political philosophy, historians of ancient politics, and policymakers interested in constitutional design
extracted.subtask_description: Examination of how governments should assign deliberative, magisterial, and judicial powers; how magistrates and judges should be chosen and organized; and what causes, mechanisms, and remedies exist for seditions and changes of government. Grounded in practical examples and principles for matching institutions to different regime-types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberative power allocation
rubrics_metrics.description: Who should hold the deliberative power in a state (people at large, magistrates, or a mixed body) and what scope of activity each should have.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Variants: allow the people a vote on proposed bills but not the right to propose contrary measures; let the people give advice while magistrates retain determining power. Also argue that pardoning and condemning powers should be distributed differently depending on regime-type (e.g., in some systems people may pardon but not condemn; in others the few pardon while the many condemn). Examples show tailoring of deliberative power to avoid disorder while giving the people some role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'magistrate'
rubrics_metrics.description: Which offices properly count as magistrates—those who are members of deliberative councils, decide causes, or command (especially command).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclude religious, choregic, heraldic, ambassadorial, economic, or servile functions from the strict civic-magistrate category unless they carry deliberative/decisional/command functions. This helps determine which roles require institutional safeguards and civic selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number and specialization of magistracies
rubrics_metrics.description: How many magistrates and offices a state should have, and whether one person should hold multiple offices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large states: allot one employment to one person (specialization improves attention and performance). Small states: a few citizens should execute many employments (practical necessity). Determine necessary versus advantageous offices and whether several charges can be entrusted to the same person without interference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Term length and reappointment rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide duration of office (six months, year, longer, perpetual) and whether a person may hold the same office multiple times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider effects of short vs long tenure and reappointment on stability, accountability, and concentration of power. Balance preventing excessive accumulation of authority with the need for experienced officers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allocation of jurisdiction (tribunal and geographic division)
rubrics_metrics.description: Which tribunals should have jurisdiction over which matters and whether jurisdiction should be tied to place, fact, or parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether matters like decency of manners should be handled by the clerk of the market when occurring in the market or by the same magistrate everywhere; whether to distinguish causes by the fact (type of offense) or by the parties (man vs woman). Allocate consistent jurisdictions to avoid confusion and conflict between magistrates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Matching magistrates to regime-type
rubrics_metrics.description: Which types of magistrates are proper to democracies, oligarchies, aristocracies, and monarchies (e.g., who is eligible and by what principle: virtue, fortune, family, wealth).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: aristocracy – offices allotted to well-educated; oligarchy – to the rich; democracy – to freemen at large. Create offices (e.g., pre-advisers) appropriate to regime needs: pre-advisers are suited to oligarchy, a senate to democracy; some offices are peculiar to particular states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of appointment (vote vs lot and their combinations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Who appoints magistrates (all citizens, some portion, or a particular order), and whether selection is by vote, by lot, or combinations thereof (including many hybrid forms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle enumerates many permutations (all elect by vote or lot; subdivisions by tribes/wards; some magistrates by lot, others by vote; some chosen from whole community, others from a class), yielding up to a dozen methods. Advice: choose modes that correspond to the nature of the community (democracy favors all electing by lot/vote; oligarchy favors selection from certain ranks and by lot; aristocracy favors selection from part by vote).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialization versus combination of magistrates' powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide which powers should be consistently assigned to the same magistrate and which should vary across places or facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether related matters (e.g., decency across locations or different sexes) should be under the same magistrate to preserve uniformity, or whether local variation is acceptable. Aim to avoid jurisdictional overlap that causes disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial structure and eight essential courts
rubrics_metrics.description: There ought to be eight kinds of courts for a well-ordered state: (1) inspection over behaviour of ex-magistrates, (2) punishment of those injuring the public, (3) causes where the state is a party, (4) disputes between magistrates and private persons appealing fines, (5) disputes about high-value contracts, (6) cases of murder (various species), (7) causes concerning strangers, and (8) small-claims court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These jurisdictions may be tried by the same or different judges depending on city size. Include special courts (e.g., Athens' Court of Phreattae for fugitives in murder cases). Small claims (one to five drachmae) should be legally determined without summoning entire body of judges. Design courts so that matters affecting public order have reliable adjudication to prevent sedition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of judges (who and how)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether judges are the whole people, some portions, and whether they are chosen by vote or lot; determine whether the same judges hear all causes or causes are split.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Four sorts arise: all people as judges in all causes; certain persons as judges in all causes; whole community in some causes but particular persons in others; or mixes. Correspondence: all-people-judges suits democracy; particular-persons judges suits oligarchy; mixed arrangements suit aristocracy or free states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Root principle of sedition: mistaken equality assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Seductions and revolutions commonly arise from incorrect extensions of equality: believing equality in one regard implies equality in all, or conversely extending inequality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish equality in number from equality in value; ensure political constitutions reflect appropriate proportional equality (some offices equal by number, others by proportionate value). Misapplied equality (or inequality) breeds sedition when expectations are frustrated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motives that incline men to sedition
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary motives for attempting to change government include desire for equality or superiority, and the aims of profit and honour (or avoiding dishonour/loss).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also list ancillary motives: haughtiness, fear, eminence, contempt, disproportionate growth in some part of the state, election intrigues, neglect, insufficient numbers, and excessive social dissimilarity. Use these categories to diagnose potential instability in a polity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ill-treatment and avarice of magistrates as causes of sedition
rubrics_metrics.description: When magistrates are haughty or seek greater profits than their office warrants—by appropriating private or public property—they provoke seditions against the state or against each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish avarice aimed at private gain versus embezzling public funds. Institutional checks and punishments for ex-magistrates (inspection courts) are necessary to deter this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excessive honours and concentration of prestige
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive honours granted to some may exceed what the state can tolerate and lead to monarchy or tyranny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preventive measures (e.g., ostracism) are preferable to corrective ones. Guard against creating individuals too great for the constitutional balance at the state's founding rather than trying to curb them later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contempt, exclusion, and coalition-building
rubrics_metrics.description: Groups excluded from administration (contempted classes, rich excluded in democracies, or poor excluded in oligarchies) may coalesce and start conspiracies or revolutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inclusion mechanisms or arenas for limited participation can reduce contempt. Beware that treating unequal persons as equal (or vice versa) in administration fosters grievance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disproportionate demographic or social growth as destabilizer
rubrics_metrics.description: A disproportionate increase in some part of the state (e.g., growth of the poor in democracies) upsets the polity's balance and predisposes to revolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor the proportional growth of social groups; maintain institutional symmetry so that no part outgrows the others to the point of challenging the constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accidental shocks and external events altering regimes
rubrics_metrics.description: Accidents (heavy war losses of a class, migrations, incorporation of outsiders) can change the composition of a city and lead to regime change without deliberate political plotting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: battles reducing nobles, admission of strangers/mercenaries into citizen rolls producing factional strife. Design resilience to demographic shocks (e.g., avoid over-dependence on a single class).

rubrics_metrics.name: Incremental neglect and gradual constitutional erosion
rubrics_metrics.description: Very small, neglected alterations—changes in election methods, census decay, or admitting unsuitable persons to offices—can silently produce large constitutional changes over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guard daily institutional practices (e.g., election procedures, census maintenance). Small procedural changes (switching from votes to lots) can be exploited by the meaner people to gain office; vigilance and procedural integrity are preventive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local/geographic and compositional friction
rubrics_metrics.description: Disagreements rooted in geography (different quarters, islands vs mainland) or in the mixing of different nations/settlers create local factions that can explode into general sedition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When founding cities or admitting new citizens, consider blending differences deliberately or providing institutions that accommodate local identities to avoid factional expulsions and long-term instability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal disputes among elites as triggers
rubrics_metrics.description: Quarrels among persons of high distinction (over marriage, inheritance, sexual slights) can escalate into full-blown sedition and overthrow governments; beginnings matter greatly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suppress and reconcile elite disputes early ('the beginning is half the business'). Institutional mechanisms for dispute resolution among the powerful reduce risk of citywide factionalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demagogues and the corruption of popular rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Demagogues who inform on property owners, distribute bribes, or pursue confiscations can provoke the wealthy to unite and overthrow democracies; in earlier eras demagogues sometimes became tyrants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for tactics: informings, bribery, shirking of public payments (e.g., trierarch obligations), and confiscations. Regulation of rhetoric, limits on confiscation powers, and preventing undue concentration of demagogic influence (e.g., by separating military command from demagoguery) can mitigate risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power accrual through military or public service as a path to regime change
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals or groups who make the state powerful (military generals, tribes, maritime forces) tend to gain influence that can translate into constitutional change or dominance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: generals gaining credit during wars, trierarchs, or maritime forces winning battles and then leading the body politic. Ensure institutional checks on military or extraordinary powers and prevent transfer of wartime prestige into unchecked civil authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanisms of revolution: violence vs fraud
rubrics_metrics.description: Revolutions occur either by direct violence (compelling submission) or by fraud (deceiving the people into consenting, then enforcing the new order).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fraud examples: promising foreign support or money to gain consent then retaining power; persuading people and then using force to maintain the change. Anticipate both forms and build transparency, credible commitments, and enforcement mechanisms to deter fraudulent transitions.
